newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says Argentina broke word over Astiz.
newsitem.headline: France says Argentina broke word over Astiz.

text.p: France said on Wednesday Argentina had broken its word by letting notorious "dirty war" navy Captain Alfredo Astiz remain active in intelligence after retiring him.
The Argentine Navy said on Tuesday that Astiz, who is wanted in France and Sweden for murder, still had a role in naval intelligence although he supposedly retired last year.

"If this is verified, it would be contrary to the spirit of assurances that Argentina gave France regarding the sidelining of this person who is responsible for the murder of two French nuns," French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told a news briefing.
Argentine Navy chief Admiral Carlos Marron said Astiz, 46, was still carrying out duties in the Navy Intelligence Service connected with foreign and domestic military intelligence.
The Astiz case has long clouded Franco-Argentine relations.
Astiz was sentenced to life in jail in France in absentia for the murder of nuns Leonie Duquet and Alice Domon in 1977 during the military junta's "dirty war" on alleged leftists.
Paris has vainly sought to have him extradited and had to be content with assurances that he had left the navy before President Jacques Chirac visited Argentina last March.
Chirac told reporters during his visit that he wished Astiz could serve his sentence in France and much regretted he had not been punished.

Sweden also wants to try Astiz for the 1977 disappearance of Swedish teenager Dagmar Hagelin. The Swedish girl and the French nuns are believed to have been killed at the Navy Mechanical School, the junta's most infamous torture centre.
Astiz, known as the "Blond Angel," became a hated symbol of military immunity from punishment for murder, kidnapping and torture under the 1976-83 dictatorship.
Tried and sentenced after democracy returned, he was freed under an amnesty for "Dirty War" officers in 1989 and forced to retire from the Navy late last year after a campaign by human rights groups.
